explanation: The rule makes the same three edits as the human: `ida_simple_get(&ctrl_ida, 0, 0, GFP_KERNEL)` becomes `ida_alloc(&ctrl_ida, GFP_KERNEL)`, and both `ida_simple_remove` calls become `ida_free`. It also migrates a fourth call, `ida_simple_get(&ctrl->laddr_ida, 0, SLIM_LA_MANAGER - 1, GFP_KERNEL)`, to `ida_alloc_max(&ctrl->laddr_ida, SLIM_LA_MANAGER - 1 - 1, GFP_KERNEL)`. The human commit left that call unmigrated (human.c line 439 still has `ida_simple_get`). The extra edit keeps the behaviour the same: `ida_simple_get` excludes the end value and `ida_alloc_max` includes its max, so the max becomes end - 1. The rule output compiled and all three build logs are empty. The rule covers every site the human changed plus one more, correctly, which is a valid alternative that differs from the human's choice.

The rule migrated all three sites the human migrated, and the output compiled. The two ida_simple_remove calls became ida_free(&ptp_clocks_map, ptp->index) and ida_free(&ptp_clocks_map, index), matching the human fix exactly. The only difference is the allocation call: the rule wrote "ida_alloc_max(&ptp_clocks_map, MINORMASK + 1 - 1, GFP_KERNEL)" and the human wrote "ida_alloc_max(&ptp_clocks_map, MINORMASK, GFP_KERNEL)". Both give the same inclusive maximum, so the rule's version only adds a redundant "+ 1 - 1".

The rule migrated the same three sites as the human. Both changed `ida_simple_remove(&port->in_hopids, hopid)` and `ida_simple_remove(&port->out_hopids, hopid)` to `ida_free(...)` with identical text. For the allocation call, the human wrote `ida_alloc_range(ida, min_hopid, max_hopid, GFP_KERNEL)` and the rule wrote `ida_alloc_range(ida, min_hopid, max_hopid + 1 - 1, GFP_KERNEL)`. That is the same value, only not simplified, and it cannot overflow because max_hopid is clamped to port_max_hopid just before. The 'divergent' label comes only from this textual difference. The rule output compiled and the commit made no other edits.

The rule migrated all 8 sites the human migrated: 3 ida_simple_get calls and 5 ida_simple_remove calls, including the two multi-line removes that were folded onto one line. The only difference is in the two range allocations. The rule wrote `ida_alloc_range(&fw_mgmt->id_map, 1, 256 - 1, GFP_KERNEL)` where the human wrote `ida_alloc_range(&fw_mgmt->id_map, 1, 255, GFP_KERNEL)`. These are the same constant, so the meaning is unchanged. The minor-number allocation (`ida_alloc_max(&fw_mgmt_minors_map, NUM_MINORS - 1, GFP_KERNEL)`) matches the human's version exactly, and the rule output compiled.

The rule migrated the only site to `ida_alloc_max(&ctrl->laddr_ida, SLIM_LA_MANAGER - 1 - 1, GFP_KERNEL)`. This keeps the old behaviour exactly, because ida_simple_get's upper bound is exclusive and ida_alloc_max's is inclusive. The human wrote `ida_alloc_max(&ctrl->laddr_ida, SLIM_LA_MANAGER - 1, GFP_KERNEL)` on purpose to change behaviour. The commit message says "this change allows one more device. Previously address 0xFE was never used" and carries a Fixes tag. So the rule's migration is valid and compiles but is a different choice from the human's; the `- 1 - 1` form is also a bit awkward.

The rule changed both sites the human changed in drivers/usb/gadget/function/rndis.c, and it compiles. The human wrote `ida_alloc_max(&rndis_ida, 999, GFP_KERNEL)`. The rule wrote `ida_alloc_max(&rndis_ida, 1000 - 1, GFP_KERNEL)`, which is the same value written differently. Both replaced `ida_simple_remove(&rndis_ida, nr)` with `ida_free(&rndis_ida, nr)`. The only difference is that the human folded the constant.

The rule rewrites the same four sites as the human fix. It turns `pci_alloc_consistent(pdev, size, dma)` into `dma_alloc_coherent(&pdev->dev, size, dma, GFP_KERNEL)`, both `pci_free_consistent` calls into `dma_free_coherent(&pdev->dev, ...)`, and `pci_zalloc_consistent(pdev, VME_CRCSR_BUF_SIZE, &bridge->crcsr_bus)` into `dma_alloc_coherent(&pdev->dev, VME_CRCSR_BUF_SIZE, &bridge->crcsr_bus, GFP_KERNEL)`. The only difference from human.c is layout: the rule puts `GFP_KERNEL` on a line of its own in the crcsr allocation. The tokens match the human's exactly, and the output compiled. The "divergent" class comes from that whitespace difference alone.

The rule's output matches the human fix at every site in drivers/firewire/nosy.c. It changes `pci_set_dma_mask(dev, ...)` to `dma_set_mask(&dev->dev, ...)`, the three `pci_alloc_consistent` calls to `dma_alloc_coherent(&lynx->pci_device->dev, ..., GFP_KERNEL)`, and all six `pci_free_consistent` calls to `dma_free_coherent(&lynx->pci_device->dev, ...)`. Running `diff -u human.c manual.c` shows only one difference, a line break: the rule puts `GFP_KERNEL);` on its own line after `&lynx->rcv_buffer_bus,`, which is formatting only. The build logs are empty and the rule's output compiled.

The rule migrated all 8 sites the human migrated, at the same lines and with the same API form. That is 3 pci_alloc_consistent calls changed to dma_alloc_coherent(&ioc->pcidev->dev, ..., GFP_KERNEL) and 5 pci_free_consistent calls changed to dma_free_coherent(&ioc->pcidev->dev, ...). The only difference is that the rule keeps the old `(u8 *)` cast on the freed pointer, for example `(u8 *)ppage0_alloc, page0_dma);`, where the human dropped it (`ppage0_alloc, page0_dma);`). Because dma_free_coherent takes a void *, the cast has no effect on behaviour. The rule's output compiled, and its build log contains no errors or warnings.

The human commit changed two sites in this file, both `pci_unmap_page((lio->oct_dev)->pci_dev, ...)`, to `dma_unmap_page(&lio->oct_dev->pci_dev->dev, ...)`. The rule's streaming rule covers pci_map_page, pci_map_single, pci_unmap_single, pci_dma_mapping_error and pci_dma_sync_sg_for_cpu, but it has no pci_unmap_page case. As a result nothing matched, and manual.c is byte-for-byte the same as before.c. Adding the same one-line pattern for pci_unmap_page to the rule would have handled both sites.

The human fix replaced the whole 64-bit-with-32-bit-fallback block with one call, `ret = dma_set_mask_and_coherent(&pdev->dev, DMA_BIT_MASK(64)); if (ret) {...}`. The rule only rewrote the two `pci_set_dma_mask(pdev, ...)` conditions to `dma_set_mask(&pdev->dev, ...)`, through the stand-alone `mask_only` fallback. It left both `pci_set_consistent_dma_mask(pdev, DMA_BIT_MASK(32/64))` calls unmigrated. Its `mask_fallback` rule only matches the assignment form `E = pci_set_dma_mask(P, M1); if (E)`, but this file tests the call directly inside the `if` condition. What the rule did change is correct, keeps the original behaviour and compiles, so the result is a partial, too-narrow migration and not a wrong one.

The rule and the human both replace the two mask calls, `pci_set_dma_mask` and `pci_set_consistent_dma_mask`, with a single `err = dma_set_mask_and_coherent(&dev->dev, DMA_BIT_MASK(32));` and drop the duplicate error block. This is the only migration site in the file, and all three build logs are empty. The one difference is which error block survives. The rule keeps the first block, which still contains `err = -EIO;`. The human keeps the second block, which does not. dma_set_mask_and_coherent only returns 0 or -EIO, so `err = -EIO;` reassigns the value err already holds and the probe returns -EIO either way. The behaviour is identical, so this is a cosmetic difference, not a different API or behaviour choice.

The rule correctly converts pci_map_page, pci_dma_mapping_error, pci_map_single, pci_unmap_single and pci_set_dma_mask, and the result compiles. It leaves all five pci_unmap_page sites unconverted, for example `pci_unmap_page(mgp->pdev, dmatest_bus, PAGE_SIZE, DMA_BIDIRECTIONAL);` and the `pci_unmap_page(pdev, ..., PCI_DMA_FROMDEVICE)` site in the rx path. It also leaves PCI_DMA_TODEVICE as the direction argument in the converted dma_unmap_single and dma_map_single calls. In the probe path it keeps `(void)pci_set_consistent_dma_mask(pdev, DMA_BIT_MASK(64));` instead of merging it into dma_set_mask_and_coherent, as the human did. Behaviour is unchanged because the PCI_DMA_* constants are aliases of the DMA_* values and the separate consistent-mask call does the same job. Still, the human migrated all of these sites, and the rule has no pci_unmap_page pattern and its mask-merge pattern does not match the non-adjacent consistent-mask call, so the migration is incomplete.

The human fix merged each mask pair in qlcnic_set_dma_mask into one call: `if (!dma_set_mask_and_coherent(&pdev->dev, DMA_BIT_MASK(64)))`, and did the same for the 32-bit mask. The rule only handles the merged pair when it is written with `||`, as in `pci_set_dma_mask(P, M) || pci_set_consistent_dma_mask(P, M)`. It has no case for the `!pci_set_dma_mask(...) && !pci_set_consistent_dma_mask(...)` form used here. So only the fallback rule (1d) fired, giving `!dma_set_mask(&pdev->dev, DMA_BIT_MASK(64)) && !pci_set_consistent_dma_mask(pdev, DMA_BIT_MASK(64))`. That change is behaviour-preserving and compiles, but both legacy pci_set_consistent_dma_mask calls are still there, so the migration of the human's sites is incomplete.

The rule correctly migrated both `pci_map_page` calls and both `pci_dma_mapping_error` calls to `dma_map_page(&hwdev->dev, ...)` and `dma_mapping_error(&hwdev->dev, ...)`, and the output compiled. It left `pci_unmap_page(hwdev, phys, PAGE_SIZE, PCI_DMA_FROMDEVICE);` unchanged, while the human changed it to `dma_unmap_page(&hwdev->dev, phys, PAGE_SIZE, DMA_FROM_DEVICE);`. The rule lists only pci_map_page, pci_map_single, pci_unmap_single, pci_dma_mapping_error and pci_dma_sync_sg_for_cpu, with no pci_unmap_page pattern. Apart from that one site, the only difference is a line break.

The rule correctly converted some calls: pci_map_page/pci_map_single to dma_map_* with &il->pci_dev->dev, pci_dma_mapping_error to dma_mapping_error, and pci_unmap_single(dev, ...) to dma_unmap_single(&dev->dev, ...). It also turned pci_set_dma_mask into dma_set_mask, and the output compiles. It missed several sites the human migrated. Four pci_unmap_page(il->pci_dev, ..., PCI_DMA_FROMDEVICE) calls are untouched, for example in il4965_rx_queue_reset and il4965_rx_handle. pci_dma_sync_single_for_cpu/for_device are untouched. Some converted calls still pass PCI_DMA_BIDIRECTIONAL/PCI_DMA_TODEVICE, as in "dma_map_single(&il->pci_dev->dev, &out_cmd->hdr, firstlen, PCI_DMA_BIDIRECTIONAL)". Finally, pci_set_consistent_dma_mask was left in place where the human folded both mask calls into dma_set_mask_and_coherent. Nothing the rule did changes behaviour (the PCI_DMA_* values equal the DMA_* enums), so the result is an incomplete but correct migration.

The rule rewrote `pci_unmap_single(data->device, ...)` as `dma_unmap_single(&data->device->dev, ...)`. `data->device` is a `void *` field in `struct xilly_mapping`, so the build fails with "xillybus_pcie.c:72:39: error: request for member 'dev' in something not a structure or union". The human commit changed that field to `struct device *device` in xillybus.h, passed `data->device` straight to `dma_unmap_single`, and set `this->device = ep->dev;` instead of `ep->pdev`. That fix depends on the header edit in another file, which a single-file syntactic rule cannot make. The rule also converted `pci_map_single` and `pci_dma_mapping_error`, which the human left alone in this commit. Those extra changes are harmless, but the output still does not compile.

The rule converts all four calls the human converted: two pci_map_single and two pci_unmap_single become dma_*_single(&...->pdev->dev, ...). It misses the constants the human also migrated. Both PCI_DMA_TODEVICE arguments stay in place ("dma_map_single(&itv->pdev->dev, ..., PCI_DMA_TODEVICE)") instead of becoming DMA_TO_DEVICE, because the rule's "direction" pass did not fire. The rule also has no case for "s->dma != PCI_DMA_NONE", which the human changed to DMA_NONE. The PCI_* macros are compat aliases with the same values, so the output still compiles and behaves the same, but those sites are only half migrated.

The rule's output for pci_map_single, pci_dma_mapping_error, pci_unmap_single and pci_set_dma_mask -> dma_set_mask(&pdev->dev, ...) matches the human's changes exactly, and the file compiles. It leaves two sites the human migrated untouched: `pci_dma_sync_single_for_cpu(pluto->pdev, ..., PCI_DMA_FROMDEVICE)` and `pci_dma_sync_single_for_device(...)`. The human changed these to `dma_sync_single_for_cpu/for_device(&pluto->pdev->dev, ..., DMA_FROM_DEVICE)`. The rule's streaming section only handles `pci_dma_sync_sg_for_cpu` and has no case for the single-buffer sync wrappers, so the rule is too narrow.

The rule handles pci_set_dma_mask, pci_free_consistent and the other wrappers exactly as the human did. It leaves 8 `pci_set_consistent_dma_mask(...)` calls unmigrated, while the human turned each into `dma_set_coherent_mask(&pdev->dev, ...)`. The rule also rewrote every `pci_alloc_consistent` to `dma_alloc_coherent(..., GFP_KERNEL)`. The human left those calls alone on purpose: the commit message says "all functions but pci_alloc_consistent() are handled. pci_alloc_consistent() needs more attention and explanation." The later commit 2d50607260a6 states "mpt_alloc_fw_memory() should still use GFP_ATOMIC", yet the rule produces `ioc->cached_fw = dma_alloc_coherent(&ioc->pcidev->dev, size, &ioc->cached_fw_dma, GFP_KERNEL)` there. That changes allocation behaviour from the GFP_ATOMIC the old wrapper used to GFP_KERNEL, which can sleep, so the rule introduced a possible bug even though the code compiles.

The rule converts only two kinds of site. It changes `pci_map_page`/`pci_dma_mapping_error` to `dma_map_page(&intel_private.pcidev->dev, ...)`/`dma_mapping_error(...)`, and it changes `pci_set_dma_mask` to `dma_set_mask`. Those edits are correct and the output compiles. It keeps `PCI_DMA_BIDIRECTIONAL` instead of `DMA_BIDIRECTIONAL`, which is harmless because the two constants have the same value. Four sites the human converted stay unchanged in the rule output: `pci_map_sg(intel_private.pcidev, st->sgl, st->nents, PCI_DMA_BIDIRECTIONAL)`, `pci_unmap_sg`, `pci_unmap_page` and the `else` branch `pci_set_consistent_dma_mask`. The rule has no patterns for the sg and unmap_page wrappers or for a standalone consistent-mask call in an `else` branch, and it only rewrites the TODEVICE/FROMDEVICE direction constants.

The rule's output is identical to before.c. The human made one edit, `-	.remove = mtk_clk_simple_remove,` to `+	.remove_new = mtk_clk_simple_remove,`. The callback is a shared helper defined in clk-mtk.c, and the human commit ("clk: mediatek: Make mtk_clk_simple_remove() return void") changed that helper to return void in that other file. The rule only switches `.remove` to `.remove_new` after it has converted a callback defined in the same file (`@depends on fn@`), so it correctly left this file alone. This explains why the human fix does not compile against the parent tree when taken alone.

The rule's output (manual.c) is identical to before.c. The rule only matches strlcpy() calls used as statements (`strlcpy(dst, src, size);`), and both sites in this file use the return value. The human migrated both, `return strlcpy(buf, p->name, buflen);` in check_mapped_name and `return strlcpy(buf, p->names[index], buflen);` in check_mapped_selector_name, by adding a local `int len` and rewriting each as `len = strscpy(...); return len < 0 ? buflen : len;`. That adapts to strscpy returning -E2BIG on truncation, which needs a judgment about what callers expect, so a purely syntactic rule cannot make it.

The file has only one strlcpy call, `len = strlcpy(rspn_req->rspn.fr_name, fc_host_symbolic_name(shost), FC_SYMBOLIC_NAME_SIZE);`. Its return value is used, so the rule leaves it alone on purpose: it only matches `strlcpy(dst, src, size);` as a whole statement. As a result, manual.c is identical to before.c. The human fix does more than swap the call. It changes the destination to `rspn_req->name` with `sizeof(rspn_req->name)`, adds two BUILD_BUG_ON size checks, and adds `if (WARN_ON(len < 0)) len = sizeof(rspn_req->name) - 1;` to handle strscpy's -E2BIG return. The commit touches only zfcp_fc.c, so this is not a multi-file dependency. Getting it right means understanding how the return value is used, which a syntactic rule cannot decide.

The rule reproduces all three of the human's edits exactly: `ida_alloc(&ctrl_ida, GFP_KERNEL)` and the two `ida_free` calls. It also rewrites a fourth site that the human left alone. That site is `ret = ida_simple_get(&ctrl->laddr_ida, 0, SLIM_LA_MANAGER - 1, GFP_KERNEL);`, which the rule turns into `ret = ida_alloc(&ctrl->laddr_ida, GFP_KERNEL);`, so the upper bound on logical addresses is lost. The cause is the generic rule `- E0 = ida_simple_get(E1, 0, E2, GFP_KERNEL); + E0 = ida_alloc(E1, GFP_KERNEL);`, which drops any max argument E2 instead of only matching 0. The code still compiles, but the allocator can now hand out addresses at or above the manager address, which changes behaviour. The correct form would have been ida_alloc_max(..., SLIM_LA_MANAGER - 2, ...).

Both ida_simple_remove sites were migrated to ida_free, the same as the human did. The allocation site is the problem. The rule's over-general pattern `- E0 = ida_simple_get(E1, 0, E2, GFP_KERNEL); + E0 = ida_alloc(E1, GFP_KERNEL);` turned `ida_simple_get(&ptp_clocks_map, 0, MINORMASK + 1, GFP_KERNEL)` into `ida_alloc(&ptp_clocks_map, GFP_KERNEL)`, which throws away the upper bound. The human wrote `ida_alloc_max(&ptp_clocks_map, MINORMASK, GFP_KERNEL)`. The rule's version compiles but changes behaviour: indices above MINORMASK can now be allocated, so they would overflow the minor number used in MKDEV.

The human fix migrated three sites. The rule handled the two removals correctly: `ida_simple_remove(&rng_index_ida, index)` and `ida_simple_remove(&rng_index_ida, vi->index)` both became `ida_free`, matching the human version exactly. It missed the allocation, `vi->index = index = ida_simple_get(&rng_index_ida, 0, 0, GFP_KERNEL);`, which the human changed to `ida_alloc(&rng_index_ida, GFP_KERNEL)`. The rule's statement-level pattern `- E0 = ida_simple_get(E1, 0, E2, GFP_KERNEL);` cannot match because this is a chained assignment: the outer right-hand side is another assignment, not the call. The changes the rule did make are correct and the output compiled, so this is a partial migration caused by a pattern that is too narrow.

The rule changes all four ida_simple_remove sites to ida_free and turns the unbounded `ida_simple_get(&rpmsg_ctrl_ida, 0, 0, GFP_KERNEL)` into `ida_alloc`, the same as the human fix. But its over-general rule `- E0 = ida_simple_get(E1, 0, E2, GFP_KERNEL); + E0 = ida_alloc(E1, GFP_KERNEL);` throws away the non-zero upper bound. It rewrote `ida_simple_get(&rpmsg_minor_ida, 0, RPMSG_DEV_MAX, GFP_KERNEL)` as the unbounded `ida_alloc(&rpmsg_minor_ida, GFP_KERNEL)`, where the human wrote `ida_alloc_max(&rpmsg_minor_ida, RPMSG_DEV_MAX - 1, GFP_KERNEL)`. That changes behaviour: minor numbers are no longer capped at MINORMASK, so MKDEV(MAJOR(rpmsg_major), ret) can overflow past the chrdev region. The file still compiles, but the change is a real bug.

The rule correctly turned both `ida_simple_remove(&port->in_hopids, hopid)` and `ida_simple_remove(&port->out_hopids, hopid)` into `ida_free(...)`, exactly as the human did. It missed the allocation site: the human changed `return ida_simple_get(ida, min_hopid, max_hopid + 1, GFP_KERNEL);` to `return ida_alloc_range(ida, min_hopid, max_hopid, GFP_KERNEL);`. That line is unchanged in the rule output. Every get-pattern in the rule needs an assignment (`E0 = ida_simple_get(...)`) and hard-codes specific arguments, so it cannot match a `return` statement or a generic min/max range with the `+ 1` removed.

The rule changed `minor = ida_simple_get(&fw_mgmt_minors_map, 0, NUM_MINORS, GFP_KERNEL);` into `minor = ida_alloc(&fw_mgmt_minors_map, GFP_KERNEL);`, which drops the upper bound. The human wrote `ida_alloc_max(&fw_mgmt_minors_map, NUM_MINORS - 1, GFP_KERNEL)`. The chrdev region is allocated with only NUM_MINORS (U8_MAX) minors, so the unbounded allocation can return a minor outside the registered region and pass it to MKDEV. That is a behaviour change, not an equivalent form. The rule's generic pattern `- E0 = ida_simple_get(E1, 0, E2, GFP_KERNEL); + E0 = ida_alloc(E1, GFP_KERNEL);` is over-generalized: it throws away E2. The rule also left both `ida_simple_get(&fw_mgmt->id_map, 1, 256, ...)` sites unmigrated, where the human used `ida_alloc_range(..., 1, 255, ...)`. All six `ida_simple_remove` to `ida_free` conversions are correct and match the human's.

The rule handled all four ida_simple_remove sites the same way the human did, changing each to ida_free. The two allocation sites are a different story. The human turned `ida_simple_get(&mmc_blk_ida, 0, max_devices, GFP_KERNEL)` and the RPMB version into `ida_alloc_max(..., max_devices - 1, GFP_KERNEL)`, which keeps the upper bound. The rule instead applied its over-general pattern `E0 = ida_simple_get(E1, 0, E2, GFP_KERNEL)` -> `ida_alloc(E1, GFP_KERNEL)` and dropped `max_devices`. Without that limit, devidx can now go past the minor-number range, and allocation no longer fails with -ENOSPC when the limit is reached, although the code's own comment depends on that. This is a behaviour change, so the result is wrong even though it compiles.

The human fix turns `ida_simple_get(&ctrl->laddr_ida, 0, SLIM_LA_MANAGER - 1, GFP_KERNEL)` into `ida_alloc_max(&ctrl->laddr_ida, SLIM_LA_MANAGER - 1, GFP_KERNEL)`, which keeps the upper bound. The spinfer output is `ret = ida_alloc(&ctrl->laddr_ida, GFP_KERNEL);`, which drops the bound completely. It came from an overgeneralized rule, `- E0 = ida_simple_get(E1, 0, E2, GFP_KERNEL); + E0 = ida_alloc(E1, GFP_KERNEL);`, that throws away any end argument E2. The code still compiles, but logical addresses can now be allocated up to INT_MAX instead of staying below SLIM_LA_MANAGER, which changes behaviour.

The human fix migrated two sites. It turned `ida_simple_remove(&guc->submission_state.guc_ids, ce->guc_id.id)` into `ida_free(...)`, and it turned `ida_simple_get(&guc->submission_state.guc_ids, NUMBER_MULTI_LRC_GUC_ID(guc), guc->submission_state.num_guc_ids, GFP_KERNEL | __GFP_RETRY_MAYFAIL | __GFP_NOWARN)` into `ida_alloc_range(..., guc->submission_state.num_guc_ids - 1, ...)`. The spinfer output reproduces the ida_free change exactly, but it leaves the ida_simple_get call untouched. Every ida_simple_get rule in the spinfer file was learned for a specific symbol or constant (cntlid_ida, phy_fixed_ida, `&E1->halloc`, and so on) or requires a literal `GFP_KERNEL` with start 0. None of them matches a general range allocation with OR'ed GFP flags and an exclusive end that has to become inclusive (end - 1). What the rule did change is correct and compiles; it is just incomplete.

The human migrated two sites: `return ida_simple_get(&rndis_ida, 0, 1000, GFP_KERNEL);` became `return ida_alloc_max(&rndis_ida, 999, GFP_KERNEL);`, and `ida_simple_remove(&rndis_ida, nr);` became `ida_free(&rndis_ida, nr);`. The rule's output changes only the remove call, using the generic `- ida_simple_remove(&E0, E1); + ida_free(&E0, E1);` rule, and that change matches the human's exactly and compiles. The get call is left unmigrated. Every ida_simple_get rule in the spinfer set expects an assignment (`E0 = ida_simple_get(...)`), and most also hard-code a specific ida name or bound. None of them matches the `return ida_simple_get(..., 0, 1000, ...)` form, and none would turn the exclusive end 1000 into the inclusive max 999.

The rule matches the human fix in vhost_vdpa_release_dev (`ida_simple_remove` -> `ida_free(&vhost_vdpa_ida, v->minor)`). At the allocation site it differs. The human wrote `ida_alloc_max(&vhost_vdpa_ida, VHOST_VDPA_DEV_MAX - 1, GFP_KERNEL)`, but the rule's over-generalised pattern `- E0 = ida_simple_get(E1, 0, E2, GFP_KERNEL); + E0 = ida_alloc(E1, GFP_KERNEL);` throws away the upper bound E2. The code compiles, but the minor number is no longer capped below VHOST_VDPA_DEV_MAX (1U << MINORBITS), which is also the size of the chrdev region passed to alloc_chrdev_region. That changes behaviour: a minor outside the reserved device range could be handed out. The right fix only needs a syntactic rewrite (max - 1), so the cause is a rule that generalised too far, not a need for semantic judgment.

The human migrated four sites. The rule handled two of them correctly: `pci_zalloc_consistent(pdev, VME_CRCSR_BUF_SIZE, &bridge->crcsr_bus)` became `dma_alloc_coherent(&pdev->dev, ..., GFP_KERNEL)`, and the CR/CSR `pci_free_consistent` became `dma_free_coherent(&pdev->dev, ...)`. Both match the human's code except for line wrapping. It left the two wrapper sites untouched: `return pci_alloc_consistent(pdev, size, dma);` and `pci_free_consistent(pdev, size, vaddr, dma);`. Those patterns are too narrow to reach them. The alloc rule only matches the assignment form `E0 = I1(E2, E3, &E4)`, not a `return` statement. The free rule needs the last two arguments to be field accesses (`E2->I3, E2->I4`), but here they are plain variables.

The rule output matches the human fix exactly for all three `pci_alloc_consistent(pci, ...)` -> `dma_alloc_coherent(&pci->dev, ..., GFP_KERNEL)` sites and for `pci_free_consistent(dev->pci, ...)` -> `dma_free_coherent(&dev->pci->dev, ...)`. It leaves `err = pci_set_dma_mask(pci_dev, 0xffffffff);` unchanged, while the human changed it to `dma_set_mask(&pci_dev->dev, 0xffffffff)`. The rule's mask patterns only match the literal `DMA_BIT_MASK(32)`/`(28)`/`(48)`/`(64)` arguments (e.g. `- E0 = pci_set_dma_mask(E1, DMA_BIT_MASK(32));`), so the raw `0xffffffff` constant is not matched.
